reading.reading_name: Guidance for Standard V: Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions

drills.los_text: demonstrate a thorough knowledge of the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct by interpreting the Code and Standards in various situations involving issues of professional integrity
drills.reading_name: Guidance for Standard V: Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions

questions.stem: Pressed to price several oil-and-gas exploration IPOs before a tax loophole closes, and short of research resources, Hawke sets each price from the issuer's relative size and plans to justify the prices later. His pricing most likely:

options.A: is adequate for the time available.
options.B: is short of the required due diligence.
options.C: is adequate for the weight issuer size carries.

rationales.A: A closing tax window creates commercial urgency but does not make a thinner analysis adequate: the diligence threshold of Standard V(A) is the same whatever time is available. If the firm cannot bring adequate resources to bear on every issue in the time it has, the appropriate response is to price fewer issues or to decline the engagement, not to substitute a size heuristic for the analysis and document a justification afterwards.
rationales.B: By categorizing the issuers by general size, Hawke bypassed researching all the other relevant aspects that must be considered when pricing new issues and thus did not perform sufficient due diligence. Standard V(A) requires members and candidates to exercise diligence, independence and thoroughness and to have a reasonable and adequate basis, supported by appropriate research and investigation, for any investment recommendation or action. Deciding the price first and assembling the justification later inverts that requirement, so Hawke violated Standard V(A).
rationales.C: Relative size is one input among many. Pricing an exploration issue also turns on reserves and resource quality, the capital programme and funding needs, management quality, comparable transactions and trading multiples, and prevailing market conditions. Treating size as a sufficient proxy for all of these leaves the recommendation without a reasonable and adequate basis.

questions.stem: Chandler screens Dalton's US equity manager database for a client. Between the screen and the delivery of her report, one of the five recommended firms loses its chief investment officer, its head of US equity research and most of its US equity portfolio managers, who leave to form their own firm. Chandler does not revise the report. She most likely:

options.A: owed the client a revised report before delivery.
options.B: owed no revision, the track record being unchanged.
options.C: owed no revision, the screen being accurate when run.

rationales.A: Chandler failed to satisfy the requirement of Standard V(A) because she did not update her report to reflect the new information. Diligence, independence and thoroughness extend to the moment of delivery: when a material event occurs between completion of the analysis and communication of the recommendation, the member or candidate must update the work so that the client receives a recommendation resting on a reasonable and adequate basis at the time it is acted upon.
rationales.B: The historical performance record was produced by the people who have just left. The departure of the chief investment officer, the head of US equity research and most of the US equity portfolio managers goes directly to whether that record remains a reasonable basis for recommending the firm, so an unchanged track record does not relieve Chandler of the need to revise.
rationales.C: Accuracy as of the search date is not the test. Standard V(A) requires the recommendation to have a reasonable and adequate basis when it is delivered, so a material event arising between the analysis and its communication obliges the analyst to revise the report rather than deliver a screen she knows to be stale.

questions.stem: A fixed-income committee revises Mastakis's rate forecast to show rates rising by more than she predicted, and she asks that her name be removed from the report. Regarding group research under Standard V(A), it is most likely that:

options.A: a dissenting analyst must normally dissociate.
options.B: an analyst must generally report his or her own opinion.
options.C: a committee may not override an analyst's forecast.

rationales.A: Removal is available to her but is not compulsory. If Mastakis is satisfied that the committee's process produced results or conclusions that have a reasonable and adequate basis, she does not have to dissociate from the report even though she disagrees with its contents. Dissociation becomes necessary only where the conclusion lacks such a basis or where her name would lend support to work she believes unfounded.
rationales.B: Generally, analysts must write research reports that reflect their own opinion. But the results of research are not always definitive, and different people may draw different opinions from the same factual evidence. When research is a group effort, not all members of the team may agree with every aspect of the report, and the committee may have valid reasons for issuing a report that differs from the analyst's original research if there is a reasonable and adequate basis for its conclusions. Ultimately, members and candidates can ask to have their names removed from the report, but if they are satisfied that the process has produced results or conclusions that have a reasonable and adequate basis, they do not have to dissociate from the report even when they do not agree with its contents. So an analyst owes the report her own opinion, yet Mastakis need not dissociate if she is confident in the committee's process.
rationales.C: Group research is permitted to reach a conclusion that differs from an individual contributor's view. Provided the committee's revised forecast rests on a reasonable and adequate basis supported by appropriate research and investigation, overriding Mastakis's original prediction is not itself a breach of Standard V(A).

questions.stem: McDermott's two-person firm subscribes to research from a large investment research firm and bases its client recommendations on those reports. Under Standard V(A), that reliance is most likely:

options.A: permitted, if the firm determines the research is sound.
options.B: prohibited, unless the firm produced the research itself.
options.C: permitted, if the firm subscribes to a reputable service.

rationales.A: Members and candidates may rely on third-party research, but they must make reasonable and diligent efforts to determine that such research is sound. If McDermott undertakes due diligence on a regular basis to confirm that the large firm's research is objective and reasonably based, she may rely on it when making investment recommendations to clients. The diligence is the recurring review of the research's assumptions, rigor and timeliness, not the act of subscribing, and the obligation is the same whatever the size of the subscribing firm.
rationales.B: Reliance on third-party research is permitted, provided the member makes reasonable and diligent efforts to establish its soundness. Standard V(A) imposes no prohibition keyed to firm size: a two-person firm may base recommendations on research it did not produce, once it has satisfied itself that the research is objective and reasonably based.
rationales.C: Subscribing to a reputable service is not itself the diligence required. What satisfies Standard V(A) is periodic review of the research's assumptions, rigor and timeliness, so that the member can show the work supporting a recommendation is sound. Paying for a well-regarded feed and passing its conclusions through untested does not meet that threshold.

questions.stem: Ostrowski uses a model request for proposal to source seven subadviser candidates, feels unqualified to choose among them, and selects the firm charging the lowest fees. Under Standard V(A), that selection is most likely:

options.A: noncompliant, because fees alone are not a full review of the adviser.
options.B: compliant, because the model request for proposal sourced the candidates.
options.C: compliant, because the lowest fee minimizes client costs.

rationales.A: The selection of an external adviser or subadviser must be based on a full and complete review of the adviser's services, performance history and cost structure. In basing the decision on the fee structure alone, Ostrowski violated Standard V(A). Feeling unqualified to choose among the seven candidates is a reason to extend the analysis or to seek help with it, not a reason to substitute a single price variable for the review the standard requires.
rationales.B: A sound sourcing process does not cure a selection made on fees alone. The model request for proposal produced the candidate list; the diligence Standard V(A) requires is the full review of each candidate's services, performance history and cost structure that should have followed, and that review was never performed.
rationales.C: Cost is one legitimate factor among several. Choosing the lowest-fee adviser without evaluating services and performance history fails the reasonable-basis requirement, because the cheapest adviser may not deliver the services the client's mandate needs. Price alone cannot establish that a subadviser is suitable.

questions.stem: Thompson, analyzing subprime mortgage-backed securities, insists on testing home price appreciation assumptions of -10%, -5% and 0% over his manager's objection that the firm's database holds no negative periods; the test reveals the securities' risk and he does not recommend purchase. His conduct is most likely:

options.A: noncompliant, because the scenarios fell outside the database.
options.B: noncompliant, because his manager's seniority governs the call.
options.C: compliant, because he recognized his model's limitations.

rationales.A: Testing beyond a limited historical record is diligence, not a violation. The database contained no negative home price appreciation periods precisely because the record was short, and a model exercised only within that observed range would never reveal how the securities behave when prices fall. Standard V(A) asks the analyst to understand the limitations of the model, which is what inputs beyond the historical trends are for.
rationales.B: Seniority does not override an analyst's judgment about the limitations of a model. Thompson's insistence on running the downside scenarios, and his decision not to recommend the securities once the test exposed their risk, are the compliant conduct here. Deferring to the manager's view that the negative assumptions were too dire would have left any recommendation without a reasonable basis.
rationales.C: Thompson understands the limitations of his model, which, combined with the limited historical information available, cannot accurately predict how the funds would perform if market conditions changed negatively. His action in running the scenario test with inputs beyond the historical trends available in the firm's databases adheres to the principles of Standard V(A), and declining to recommend the purchase once the test exposed the risk follows from that analysis.

questions.stem: Carapalis intends to implement a commodity volatility derivative strategy as an integrated whole. Liakos's modeling group outsources the components to trusted third parties, he validates each component individually as it is completed and implements it, and the assembled strategy fails. Regarding Standard V(A), Liakos most likely:

options.A: complied, because each component was individually validated.
options.B: violated, because the assembled strategy was never tested.
options.C: complied, because the specialists tested their own components.

rationales.A: Validating each component in isolation was not enough. Because the client intended to implement the strategy as an integrated whole, Liakos had to test how the components interacted, and no amount of component-level validation substitutes for testing the assembled model the client would actually use.
rationales.B: Liakos violated Standard V(A). Members and candidates must understand the statistical significance of the results of the models they recommend and must be able to explain them to clients. Liakos did not take adequate care to ensure a thorough review of the whole model; its components were evaluated only individually. Because Carapalis clearly intended to implement the strategy as a whole rather than as separate parts, to comply with the standard Liakos should have tested how the components of the strategy interacted in addition to how they performed individually.
rationales.C: Outsourcing to trusted specialists who test their own pieces does not relieve Liakos of the duty to understand and test the integrated model he recommends. The diligence obligation attaches to the person making the recommendation, so the third parties' own validation cannot stand in for his review of the strategy as a whole.

questions.stem: An aggressive-profile client asks Newbury about the Top Shelf hedge fund, a long/short energy fund that returned 20% for three years using extensive leverage. Newbury analyzes the fund's track record, principals, fees and risk profile and recommends it; six months later the fund loses 60% of its value and suspends operations. Regarding Standard V(A), Newbury most likely:

options.A: complied, because his analysis gave him a reasonable basis.
options.B: violated, because the later loss shows no reasonable basis.
options.C: violated, because the fund's leverage made its risk excessive.

rationales.A: Newbury's actions were consistent with Standard V(A). Analysis of an investment that results in a reasonable basis for a recommendation does not guarantee that the investment has no downside risk. He reviewed the fund's track record, principals, fees and risk profile for a client whose stated profile was aggressive. Newbury must discuss the analysis process with the client while reminding the client that past performance does not lead to guaranteed future gains and that losses in an aggressive investment portfolio should be expected.
rationales.B: A reasonable basis does not guarantee against downside risk, and a later loss does not retroactively establish a diligence failure. Judging the recommendation by its outcome rather than by the analysis available when it was made is outcome bias. The standard asks what work supported the recommendation, and that work was done.
rationales.C: The client's aggressive mandate and Newbury's documented analysis of the track record, principals, fees and risk profile gave him a reasonable basis. Extensive leverage is a risk characteristic to analyze and disclose, not a breach of Standard V(A) in itself, so recommending a leveraged long/short fund to a client who sought that risk is not a violation.

questions.stem: Cannon, a quantitative analyst under pressure to improve his hedge fund's model, reads intriguing research on a blog run by an author calling himself Expert CFA, incorporates its factors into the firm's model, and passes the updated output's new investment recommendations to the portfolio managers. He most likely:

options.A: complied, because the blog research was publicly available.
options.B: violated only Standard I(C), because he did not cite the blog.
options.C: violated Standard V(A), because he lacked a reasonable basis.

rationales.A: Public availability does not confer a reasonable basis. The factors were taken from the blog and deployed in the firm's proprietary model without independent research into what they do, so the recommendations that followed rested on untested inputs however freely the source could be read.
rationales.B: Attribution is a separate matter. Even with the blog fully credited, the Standard V(A) failure remains: recommendations reached the portfolio managers on an untested, unvalidated basis.
rationales.C: Cannon violated Standard V(A) by failing to have a reasonable basis for the new recommendations made to the portfolio managers. He needed to research diligently the effect of incorporating the new factors before offering the output's recommendations. He may use the blog for ideas, but it is his responsibility to determine their effect on the firm's proprietary models, and pressure to improve the model does not lower that threshold.

questions.stem: Stefansson, a performance analyst asked to review five new performance attribution systems, recommends one on the strength of an impressive discussion at a conference exhibitor's booth, without researching the other four. Under Standard V(A), his recommendation is most likely:

options.A: deficient, because provider selection demands the rigor of investment analysis.
options.B: beyond the standard's reach, because provider selection is administrative.
options.C: adequate, because the booth discussion was itself research.

rationales.A: The selection of a service provider requires the same rigor as investment analysis: a full review of the provider's services, capabilities and cost structure. Members and candidates must review external providers as diligently as they review individual investment opportunities. Basing a recommendation on impressions from a single booth discussion, without researching the other four options, does not meet the reasonable-basis threshold under Standard V(A).
rationales.B: Choosing a service provider is not exempt as an administrative matter. Selecting providers demands the same rigor as investment analysis, so the full review of services, capabilities and costs is required here as well.
rationales.C: An impressive conference discussion is familiarity, not the full review of services, capabilities and costs that diligence requires. Four alternatives were never examined, so there is no comparative basis for concluding that the recommended system is the right one.

questions.stem: Willier, a research analyst whose documented outlook on Company X supports a weak hold, overhears an analyst from another firm at lunch offering conflicting opinions, returns to the office and releases a strong buy recommendation. He most likely:

options.A: violated, because he did not distinguish fact from opinion.
options.B: complied, because another analyst's opinion justified the change.
options.C: violated, because he had no reasonable basis for the change.

rationales.A: Members and candidates must distinguish between facts and opinions in their recommendations, but Willier's conduct does not illustrate a violation of that nature. The defect is that he moved a documented weak hold to a strong buy with no basis of his own for the change.
rationales.B: An opinion overheard at lunch is not a basis. Willier released a strong buy that contradicted his own documented outlook without performing any research to support the change, so the recommendation was not in compliance.
rationales.C: Willier violated the standards because he did not have a reasonable and adequate basis for his recommendation. The opinion of another financial analyst is not an adequate basis for changing a recommendation. If the opinion he overheard had sparked him to conduct additional research and investigation that justified a change of opinion, then a changed recommendation would be appropriate; acting on the remark alone was not.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(A), secondary research is most likely:

options.A: conducted by entities outside the member's own firm.
options.B: exempt from a soundness review.
options.C: conducted by someone else inside the member's firm.

rationales.A: This reverses the two terms. Research conducted by entities outside the member's or candidate's firm, such as a brokerage firm, bank or research firm, is third-party research; secondary research is produced within the member's own firm.
rationales.B: Origin inside the firm confers no exemption. If members and candidates rely on secondary or third-party research, they must make reasonable and diligent efforts to determine that such research is sound, and that duty applies equally to work produced by a colleague.
rationales.C: Secondary research is research conducted by someone else in the member's or candidate's firm. Third-party research is research conducted by entities outside the member's or candidate's firm, such as a brokerage firm, bank or research firm. If members and candidates rely on secondary or third-party research, they must make reasonable and diligent efforts to determine that such research is sound.

questions.stem: A member has reason to suspect that secondary or third-party research comes from a source that may be biased, unreliable or otherwise deficient. Under Standard V(A), the member most likely:

options.A: may rely on it unless the source is sell-side research.
options.B: must not rely on it until its soundness is established.
options.C: may rely on it if the firm subscribes to the service.

rationales.A: The soundness requirement reaches any secondary or third-party input, whether it is sell-side research, independent research or a data service. What matters is the reason to suspect the source, not the category of provider it belongs to.
rationales.B: If a member or candidate has reason to suspect that either secondary or third-party research or information comes from a source that may be biased, unreliable or otherwise deficient, the member or candidate must not rely on that information. The duty is not discharged by disclosing the doubt or by caveating the output: the suspect material must be set aside, or its soundness established independently, before it can support a recommendation.
rationales.C: A subscription is no cure for a suspected defect in the source. Reason to suspect bias, unreliability or other deficiency means the member must not rely on that information, however it was obtained and whatever it cost.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(A), a member's reliance on third-party research that the firm's senior managers selected through their own due diligence is most likely permitted:

options.A: in good faith, absent reason to question the research.
options.B: in good faith, even after the firm's own vetting has lapsed.
options.C: subject to the member re-performing the firm's due diligence.

rationales.A: Members and candidates may rely on others in their firm to determine whether secondary or third-party research is sound, and may use that information in good faith, unless they have reason to question its validity or the processes and procedures used by those responsible for the research. Portfolio managers frequently have no choice of which data source to use, because the firm's senior managers conducted the due diligence that determined which vendor would supply the information or research services. A member or candidate in that position can use the information in good faith, assuming the due diligence process was deemed adequate.
rationales.B: Reliance in good faith is conditional, not unconditional: it holds unless the member has reason to question the validity of the information or the processes and procedures behind it. A lapse in the firm's vetting of the vendor supplies exactly that reason, so the condition fails and the protection ends. From that point the member must raise the lapse with those responsible, or satisfy himself about the inputs another way, before using the research to support a recommendation.
rationales.C: Standard V(A) does not condition reliance on the member re-performing the firm's due diligence. Members and candidates may rely on colleagues' determination that secondary or third-party research is sound and use the information in good faith, provided nothing gives them reason to question its validity or the processes and procedures used by those responsible for the research. A duty to personally re-verify the sources before every use would be unworkable where the firm's senior managers chose the vendor and the portfolio manager has no choice of data source, and it is not what the standard asks.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(A), a member who incorporates a quantitative model into an investment recommendation is most likely required to:

options.A: master the model's construction, coding and underlying mathematics.
options.B: understand the model's parameters, assumptions and limitations.
options.C: confirm only the firm's approval and testing of the model.

rationales.A: The requirement is understanding, not technical authorship. Members and candidates who use quantitative models and quantitative research in their recommendations are not required to become experts in every technical aspect of those models, still less to be able to build them; what they must understand are the parameters used, the assumptions and limitations inherent in any model, and how the model's results are used in the decision-making process. The deeper technical bar applies to those who develop and oversee the models, not to those who use the analytical output.
rationales.B: Members and candidates must understand the parameters used in models and quantitative research that are incorporated into their investment recommendations. Although they are not required to become experts in every technical aspect of the models, they must understand the assumptions and limitations inherent in any model and how the results are used in the decision-making process.
rationales.C: Firm approval of a model does not displace the individual duty, and confirming that the firm approved and tested it is not the whole of what is required. A member who relies on a model's output to support a recommendation must still understand the parameters that drive it and the assumptions and limitations built into it; without that understanding the member cannot judge whether the recommendation rests on a reasonable and adequate basis, which is what Standard V(A) requires of the member personally. The firm's approval and testing speak to the firm's diligence, not to the user's understanding.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(A), the level of diligence owed in reviewing a new quantitative model is most likely:

options.A: higher for the users of the model than for its creators.
options.B: the same for the creators as for the users.
options.C: higher for the model's creators than for its users.

rationales.A: The asymmetry runs the other way. The deeper duty sits with those who design, build and oversee the model, because they are the ones positioned to understand its technical workings and to test it before anyone relies on the output. Users of the completed product owe diligence as well, but a lower level of it than the creators owe.
rationales.B: The two levels are not identical. Creators of new quantitative models and services must exhibit a higher level of diligence in reviewing new products than the individuals who ultimately use the analytical output, since the creators alone are in a position to understand the technical aspects of what they have built and to test it before distribution.
rationales.C: Individuals who create new quantitative models and services must exhibit a higher level of diligence in reviewing new products than that of the individuals who ultimately use the analytical output. Members and candidates involved in the development and oversight of quantitatively oriented models, methods and algorithms must understand the technical aspects of the products, and a thorough testing of the model and the resulting analysis must be completed prior to product distribution. The creators are the only ones positioned to do that testing before anyone relies on the output, which is why the heavier duty sits with them.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(A), a member whose financial model draws its inputs from a historical database is most likely required to:

options.A: verify the length of the data span, without regard to its source.
options.B: consider both the source and the time horizon of the data.
options.C: treat the database as spanning the full market cycle.

rationales.A: The length of the data span is not the only question, and the source cannot be left out of account. The standard requires members and candidates to consider both the source and the time horizon of the data used as inputs in financial models, so checking that the history is long enough while leaving the source unexamined meets only half the requirement. A long series drawn from a database that never saw a stressed market is still a poor input.
rationales.B: Members and candidates must also consider the source and the time horizon of the data used as inputs in financial models. Information from databases may not effectively incorporate both positive and negative market cycles, so in the development of a recommendation the member or candidate may need to test the models by using volatility and performance expectations that represent scenarios outside the observable databases.
rationales.C: A historical database cannot be assumed to span the full cycle. The information in such databases may not effectively incorporate both positive and negative market cycles, which is precisely why the standard directs the member or candidate to consider the source and the time horizon of the inputs and, where necessary, to test the model using volatility and performance expectations representing scenarios outside the observable data.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(A), a member named on a group research report whose consensus conclusion he does not share is most likely:

options.A: required to dissociate from the report, given his disagreement with it.
options.B: required to append a separate statement, given his dissenting view.
options.C: free to remain named, given an adequate, independent and objective basis.

rationales.A: Disagreement by itself does not compel dissociation. Where the member or candidate believes the consensus opinion has a reasonable and adequate basis and is independent and objective, there is no need to dissociate from the report or to ask for a name to be removed, even though the report does not reflect that member's own opinion. Dissociation is called for when the basis is not reasonable and adequate, or when the work is not independent and objective.
rationales.B: The conclusions or recommendations of a group report represent the consensus of the group, not necessarily the views of every member or candidate whose name appears on it, and the standard requires no separate dissent section or statement of individual views. What matters is whether the consensus opinion has a reasonable and adequate basis and is independent and objective, not whether each contributor's position is recorded.
rationales.C: When research is a group effort, the conclusions or recommendations of a group report represent the consensus of the group but not necessarily the views of a member or candidate, even though the name of the member or candidate is included on the report. In some instances a member or candidate will not agree with the view of the group. If, however, the member or candidate believes that the consensus opinion has a reasonable and adequate basis and is independent and objective, the member or candidate does not need to dissociate from the report even if it does not reflect his or her own opinion. Both halves of that condition matter: an adequate basis that was not reached independently and objectively would not support staying with the report.

questions.stem: Alphonso's firm, ABC Capital, charges the portfolio companies of its private equity fund for advice on structuring investments, remitting those fees to the fund when an investment falls in value but retaining them when it rises; the fund's offering memorandum does not mention the arrangement, and its investors are sophisticated institutions. Under Standard V(B), Alphonso most likely:

options.A: complied, given the sophistication of the fund's investors.
options.B: violated the standard, given the memorandum's silence on the fees.
options.C: complied, given that fees are remitted on losing investments.

rationales.A: Alphonso may not rely on the sophistication of clients and their assumed understanding of the nature and details of the fee arrangements with the underlying companies in which ABC Capital invests as a reason for not providing the information this standard requires. Sophistication changes what investors are capable of evaluating; it does not relieve the manager of the duty to disclose the compensation it receives from the fund's portfolio companies.
rationales.B: Alphonso is in violation of Standard V(B) because the compensation received by ABC Capital has not been disclosed to clients who are investors in the fund, and the offering memorandum's silence leaves them no other way to learn of it. He may not rely on the sophistication of clients and their assumed understanding of the nature and details of the fee arrangements with the underlying companies in which ABC Capital invests as a reason for not providing the information required by this standard. That is so even though investors in the fund benefit from the arrangement: fees remitted to the fund on investments that fall in value accrue to the investors, yet the arrangement as a whole still pays ABC Capital for advice given to companies the fund owns, and that compensation is information investors need in order to understand the basis on which their manager is paid.
rationales.C: The conditionality of the remittance policy is itself the thing investors need disclosed. Fees are returned to the fund when an investment declines but kept by ABC Capital when it appreciates, so on successful deals the structuring fees are compensation to the manager from companies the fund owns. Partial remittance does not remove the arrangement from the scope of Standard V(B), and the offering memorandum's silence on it leaves investors unable to evaluate how their manager is paid.

questions.stem: Jones ranks three candidate core fixed-income managers, presenting their performance gross of fees for a uniform comparison together with the total fees for each period, each manager's fee schedule and the additional fees each charges; her top-ranked candidate charges significantly higher fees than the others. Under Standard V(B), Jones most likely:

options.A: complied, given the uniform comparison and the fee disclosures.
options.B: violated the standard, given her use of gross-of-fees performance.
options.C: violated the standard, given her ranking of a costlier manager first.

rationales.A: Jones's presentation of manager fees is appropriate because she provided a uniform comparison of manager services. Her presentation adheres to Standard V(B), which requires disclosure about the nature of the services provided along with information about the costs associated with those services. Showing each candidate gross of fees puts the three on a single basis, and she paired that comparison with the total fees calculated for each period, each manager's fee schedule and the additional fees each charges, so the client can see what the top-ranked manager's significantly higher fee buys and decide whether it is worth paying.
rationales.B: Gross-of-fees figures do not overstate results when they are identified as gross and accompanied by complete fee information. Jones used them to put three managers with different fee structures on a uniform basis, and she calculated total fees for each period and listed every fee schedule and additional fee, so the client can carry the comparison through to net terms. That satisfies Standard V(B), which asks for disclosure of the nature of the services and the costs associated with them.
rationales.C: Standard V(B) requires that the costs associated with the services be disclosed alongside the nature of those services; it does not make fees the controlling selection criterion. Jones was entitled to rank the candidates on their merits and place the more expensive manager first, provided the client was told in full what that manager charges, which is what her fee schedules, period fee totals and additional-fee disclosures accomplish.

questions.stem: Maalouf's firm, whose client agreements reserve the right to revise its fee methodology, disclosed at the outset how it values assets and calculates advisory fees; it has since moved from average daily balance to end-of-cycle market value and brought previously excluded cash and cash equivalents into the fee base, lowering the fee for some clients, without telling existing clients. Under Standard V(B), Maalouf most likely:

options.A: complied, given that the revised method can lower a client's fee.
options.B: violated the standard, given the silence toward clients.
options.C: complied, given the discretion reserved over fee methodology.

rationales.A: A change in the fee calculation methodology must be disclosed whether it raises or lowers the charge. Advisory fees are critical information that clients need to know, and it is improper to change the methodology without disclosure even if the change results in lower fees for some clients. The client's right to know how the fee is computed does not depend on the direction in which the revision happens to move the number.
rationales.B: Advisory fees are critical information that clients need to know. Maalouf and his firm may change the advisory fee calculation methodology and policies over time for existing accounts, including the move from the average daily balance to the end-of-cycle market value and the decision to bring cash and cash equivalents into the fee base, but Maalouf must make clients aware of any such change. Making the changes silently violates Standard V(B); it is improper to change the fee calculation methodology without disclosure even if the result is lower fees for some clients.
rationales.C: The firm does have discretion to revise how it values assets and calculates fees for existing accounts, but discretion over the method is not discretion over disclosure. Maalouf must make clients aware of any such change, because advisory fees are critical information that clients need to know, so revising the valuation basis and widening the fee base in silence violates Standard V(B).

questions.stem: Williamson, the marketing director at Country Technicians, plans a newsletter for clients that, for simplicity, will carry only the week's five strongest buy and sell recommendations and will leave out the firm's valuation models and the details of how it structures portfolios. Under Standard V(B), Williamson's plan most likely:

options.A: violates the standard, given the omission of the firm's process.
options.B: complies, given that the simplified format better serves clients.
options.C: complies, given that brief recommendation lists are exempt.

rationales.A: Williamson's plans for the newsletter violate Standard V(B). She need not describe the investment system in detail in order for clients to implement the advice effectively, but she must inform clients of Country Technicians' basic process. Without understanding the basis for a recommendation, clients cannot evaluate its limitations or the risks inherent in it, and a weekly list of five buys and five sells stripped of the valuation models and the portfolio structuring that produced it gives them nothing to evaluate.
rationales.B: A condensed format is permissible; dropping the basis for the recommendations is not. Williamson need not set out the investment system in detail, but she must convey the firm's basic process, because clients who do not understand how a recommendation was reached cannot judge its limitations or the risks it carries. Serving a preference for brevity does not displace that requirement.
rationales.C: There is no exemption for abbreviated formats. Whatever the length of the publication, Standard V(B) requires that clients be told the basic process behind the recommendations so that they can evaluate the limitations and the inherent risks, and Williamson could satisfy that in a few lines while noting that the fuller analysis is available.

questions.stem: Dox, a mining analyst, calculates from Boisy Bay Minerals' latest core samples that the property holds 500,000 ounces of gold and closes his report with: 'Based on the fact that the company has 500,000 ounces of gold to be mined, I recommend a strong buy.' Under Standard V(B), Dox most likely:

options.A: violated the standard, given that an estimate was presented as fact.
options.B: complied, given that he calculated the reserve figure himself.
options.C: complied, given that he relied on the company's sample data.

rationales.A: Dox violated Standard V(B). His calculation of the total gold reserves for the property based on the company's recent sample drilling is a quantitative opinion, not a fact, and opinion must be distinguished from fact in research reports. Writing that the recommendation rests on the fact that the company has 500,000 ounces of gold to be mined presents a figure inferred from a limited set of core samples as an established quantity, which leaves the reader unable to see that the strong buy depends on an estimate and on the assumptions behind it.
rationales.B: Performing the calculation himself does not convert its output into a fact. A reserve figure extrapolated from recent sample drilling is a quantitative opinion, and it must be presented as an estimate, with the sampling and the assumptions it rests on made visible, so that the reader can judge how much weight the recommendation can bear. Opinion must be distinguished from fact in research reports.
rationales.C: The breach is not Dox's reliance on the company's latest core samples, which may be entirely reasonable as a starting point; it is his presentation of an estimate derived from those samples as a fact. Opinion must be distinguished from fact in a research report, and a total reserve figure extrapolated from sample drilling is a quantitative opinion however sound the underlying data.

questions.stem: Thomas's report on a structured product describes a strategy that benefits from an expected decline in interest rates, cites the product's proprietary nature, and does not explain how the firm may generate the stated returns, what risks accompany them, or how the strategy would perform if rates rose. Under Standard V(B), the report is most likely:

options.A: deficient in describing the strategy's risks.
options.B: deficient in omitting a historical performance table.
options.C: compliant with Standard V(B).

rationales.A: Thomas violated Standard V(B) because her report fails to describe properly the basic characteristics of the actual and implied risks of the investment strategy, including how the structure was created and the degree to which leverage was embedded in the structure. The report must include a balanced discussion of how the strategy would perform in the case of both rising and falling interest rates, preferably illustrating how the strategy might be expected to perform in the event of a reasonable variety of interest rate and credit risk–spread scenarios. If liquidity issues are relevant to the valuation of either the derivatives or the underlying securities, Thomas must address those risks as well. Citing the proprietary nature of the structure does not relieve her of any of these obligations.
rationales.B: The deficiency is not a missing performance table but the absent discussion of risk and of the factors driving the strategy, including how the structure was created, how much leverage it embeds, and how it would behave if rates rose rather than fell.
rationales.C: Protecting proprietary detail does not excuse failing to describe the basic characteristics and the actual and implied risks of the strategy, so the report remains deficient under Standard V(B) rather than compliant with it.

questions.stem: Clio, chief investment officer of May & Associates, an aggressive growth small-cap US equity manager whose assets under management have grown to $20 billion, raises the firm's maximum market-cap limit from $2 billion to $8 billion and revises the sales and marketing literature sent to prospective clients accordingly, but tells existing clients nothing. Under Standard V(B), Clio is most likely required to notify:

options.A: prospective clients only.
options.B: existing clients as well.
options.C: neither existing nor prospective clients.

rationales.A: Informing prospective clients and consultants is not sufficient. Existing clients hired the firm for a $2 billion small-cap discipline, and Standard V(B) requires that they be told the ceiling has moved to $8 billion.
rationales.B: Although Clio appropriately informs potentially interested parties about the change in investment process, he must also notify May's existing clients. Among the latter group might be a number of clients who not only retained May as a small-cap manager but also retained mid-cap specialists in a multiple-manager approach. Such clients may regard May's change of criteria as a style change that distorts their overall asset allocations, which is precisely why the change has to be communicated to them.
rationales.C: Quadrupling the investable market-cap ceiling changes the investment process materially rather than being a portfolio-level tactic, so Standard V(B) requires notification rather than permitting silence toward every group.

questions.stem: Clio, chief investment officer of the small-cap US equity manager May & Associates, extends the firm's small-cap universe to include non-US companies. Under Standard V(B), Clio is most likely required to:

options.A: make no disclosure of the change.
options.B: advise the firm's clients of the change.
options.C: update the firm's marketing materials.

rationales.A: Some clients may have retained May specifically for its expertise in US small-cap stocks, so extending the universe beyond the United States is a change in the investment process that must be disclosed rather than passed over in silence.
rationales.B: Standard V(B) requires Clio to advise May's clients of this change because the firm may have been retained by some clients specifically for its prowess at investing in US small-cap stocks. Clio must disclose changes in the investment process to all interested parties, which includes the firm's existing clients and not merely those considering it.
rationales.C: Refreshing marketing materials reaches prospective clients but does not discharge the duty to advise existing clients of a change in the investment process.

questions.stem: Rodriguez's firm, an active value-style equity manager, applies four multifactor valuation models. Rodriguez replaces its simple price-to-trailing-12-month-earnings model with a new dividend discount model driven by projected inflation, earnings growth, and interest rates. Under Standard V(B), Rodriguez is most likely required to:

options.A: obtain written client consent before using the model.
options.B: continue without notifying clients.
options.C: communicate the change to the firm's clients.

rationales.A: Standard V(B) imposes a duty to communicate the material change in the investment process to clients. It does not condition use of the new model on written client consent.
rationales.B: A new and different valuation model is a material change rather than a refinement. The replacement model depends at least partly on the firm's own forecasts of inflation, earnings growth, and interest rates instead of on the hard trailing-earnings data it supersedes, so adding it to an already multifactor process does not make it cosmetic, and it cannot be adopted without telling clients.
rationales.C: Because the introduction of a new and different valuation model represents a material change in the investment process, Rodriguez must communicate the change to the firm's clients. The firm is replacing a model based on hard data with a new model that is at least partly dependent on its own forecasting skills. This is a significant change rather than a mere refinement of the firm's process.

questions.stem: At Morales's firm, responsibility for selecting the stocks on the approved list shifts from individual security analysts to a committee composed of the research director and three senior portfolio managers. Morales believes the change is not important enough to communicate to her clients. Under Standard V(B), Morales is most likely required to:

options.A: make no disclosure to her clients.
options.B: disclose the change to all of her clients.
options.C: disclose the change if the committee's picks underperform.

rationales.A: Moving stock-selection authority from individual analysts to a committee is a fundamental change in how the fund is managed, not a matter of internal governance that clients have no interest in, so it is disclosable.
rationales.B: Standard V(B) requires Morales to disclose the process change to all her clients because this is a fundamental change to stock selection for the fund. Shifting the approved list from individual security analysts to a committee of the research director and three senior portfolio managers alters the investment process itself, and clients are entitled to that information whatever Morales's own view of its importance.
rationales.C: The disclosure obligation is triggered by the change in the investment process itself, not by any subsequent difference in performance between the committee's selections and the analysts', so it cannot be made to wait on results.

questions.stem: Chinn is the investment director at Diversified Asset Management, which decides to limit its direct investing to large-cap securities and to obtain small-cap and mid-cap exposure by hiring outside fund managers. Chinn's update letter to a charity endowment client describes the planned strategy change, the reasons for it, and the characteristics of the external managers. Under Standard V(B), that disclosure is most likely:

options.A: required.
options.B: required for prospective clients only.
options.C: optional.

rationales.A: Standard V(B) requires the disclosure of the investment process used to construct the portfolio of the endowment fund. Changing the investment process from managing all classes of investments within the firm to the use of external managers is an example of information about the investment process that must be communicated to clients. With Chinn's letter in hand, the charity can make a reasonable decision about whether Diversified Asset Management remains the appropriate manager for its endowment.
rationales.B: The change in the investment process must be communicated to existing clients such as the charity so that they can reassess whether the manager is still appropriate for them, and not only to prospective clients weighing the strategy.
rationales.C: Replacing in-house management of small-cap and mid-cap assets with external managers changes the investment process used to construct the client's portfolio, which Standard V(B) requires be communicated rather than left to the manager's discretion as an operational detail.

questions.stem: Yakovlev manages a small-cap quantitative strategy that he believes can absorb no more than roughly $3 billion before the capacity limit materially affects returns; the fund currently markets about $100 million. Wellard, the head of marketing, directs that the offering material address solely the strategy's track record, and Yakovlev does not object because the threshold is far away. Under Standard V(B), Yakovlev and Wellard have most likely:

options.A: presented the offering material appropriately.
options.B: had no duty to disclose the capacity limit yet.
options.C: failed to disclose a significant limitation.

rationales.A: Offering material may of course present the strategy's track record, but confining it to the track record does not excuse omitting the capacity limitation, which is a significant limitation associated with the investment product that current and prospective investors must be made aware of.
rationales.B: A known capacity limit that Yakovlev believes will materially affect returns once reached must be disclosed even while the fund markets only $100 million against a $3 billion soft threshold. Distance from the limit affects when it bites, not whether investors are entitled to know about it now.
rationales.C: Yakovlev and Wellard have not appropriately disclosed a significant limitation associated with the investment product. Yakovlev believes this limitation, once reached, will materially affect the returns of the fund. Although the fund is currently far from the $3 billion mark, current and prospective investors must be made aware of this capacity issue, and Yakovlev's failure to object to marketing material confined to the track record does not relieve him of that duty.

questions.stem: Ramon, a risk analyst, assures clients that his firm's process of calculating value at risk at a 99% confidence level over a 20-day holding period, using a methodology based on ex ante Monte Carlo simulation, is extremely effective, noting that the firm has never suffered losses greater than the analysis predicted. Under Standard V(B), Ramon has most likely:

options.A: described the model's coverage accurately.
options.B: relied appropriately on the model's loss record.
options.C: failed to communicate the risks of the process.

rationales.A: A 99% confidence level says nothing about the magnitude of losses in the remaining outcomes, so a blanket assurance of effectiveness misstates what a value at risk figure at any confidence level can promise. The limitations of the model and the risks it leaves unmeasured still have to be communicated.
rationales.B: The firm's never having lost more than the model predicted is not a substitute for communicating how the model's inputs were chosen, what the framework's limitations are, and what tail risk it does not capture, so that record cannot be leaned on as Ramon leans on it.
rationales.C: Ramon has not sufficiently communicated the risks associated with the investment process to satisfy the requirements of Standard V(B). The losses predicted by a value at risk analysis depend greatly on the inputs used in the model, and the size and probability of losses can differ significantly from what an individual model predicts. Ramon must disclose how the inputs were selected and the potential limitations and risks associated with the investment strategy rather than characterize the process as extremely effective.

questions.stem: Scott expects Walkton Industries to raise its dividend by $1.50 a share, contingent on pending tax legislation. His research report states that he expects the stock price to rise by at least $8.00 a share by year-end because the dividend will increase by $1.50 a share, and that investors should expect a total return of at least 15%. Scott has most likely violated the Standards by:

options.A: failing to separate opinion from fact.
options.B: relying on uncertain future government action.
options.C: using material nonpublic information.

rationales.A: Scott issued a research report stating that he expects the price of Walkton Industries stock to rise by $8 a share because the dividend will increase by $1.50 per share. He made this statement knowing that the dividend will increase only if Congress enacts certain legislation, an uncertain prospect. By stating that the dividend will increase, Scott failed to separate fact from opinion, which is the violation here.
rationales.B: It may be acceptable to base a recommendation, in part, on an expectation of future events even though they may be uncertain. The fault is not the reliance on pending legislation but the presentation of the contingent dividend increase as settled fact.
rationales.C: Information about whether the legislation will pass is conjecture rather than material nonpublic information, so no inside-information violation arises from Scott's use of it.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(B), the communications that must carry the required disclosures about the investment process are most likely:

options.A: formal written research reports.
options.B: any means of conveying a recommendation.
options.C: written and electronic communications.

rationales.A: For the purposes of Standard V(B), communication is not confined to a written report of the type traditionally generated by an analyst researching a security, company, or industry, so limiting the obligation to formal research reports understates its reach.
rationales.B: For the purposes of Standard V(B), communication is not confined to a written report of the type traditionally generated by an analyst researching a security, company, or industry. A presentation of information can be made via any means of communication, including in-person recommendations or descriptions, electronic communications, social media posts, or media broadcasts.
rationales.C: In-person recommendations and telephone or other oral communications fall squarely within the standard and carry the same disclosure duties as written and electronic ones, so this set is too narrow.

questions.stem: With respect to complex quantitative analyses, Standard V(B) is best described as:

options.A: permitting facts and assumptions to be blended when sources are cited.
options.B: requiring opinion to be separated from fact.
options.C: applying only to written reports, not oral recommendations.

rationales.A: Standard V(B) requires opinion and fact to be clearly distinguished, not merely sourced. Citing the source of an assumption does not tell the client which parts of the analysis are measurement and which are statistical conjecture, so blending the two remains a violation even where every source is disclosed.
rationales.B: Standard V(B) requires that opinions be separated from facts. Violations occur when members and candidates fail to separate the past from the future by not indicating that earnings estimates, changes in the outlook for dividends, or future market price information are opinions subject to future circumstances. In the case of complex quantitative analyses, members and candidates must clearly separate fact from statistical conjecture and must identify the known limitations of an analysis. Caution is also required when promoting the perceived accuracy of any model or process, because the ultimate output is merely an estimate of future results and not a certainty.
rationales.C: Standard V(B) applies to all communications with clients and prospective clients, oral as well as written. The medium does not change the duty: an analyst presenting model output in a meeting must separate fact from conjecture exactly as a written report would.

questions.stem: Within an investment firm, Standard V(B) most likely applies to:

options.A: all employees, including operations and technology staff.
options.B: members whose firms have retail clients.
options.C: client-facing members only.

rationales.A: The standard centers on those who prepare or communicate research, recommendations and the accompanying disclosures, not on every member of staff. Operations and technology employees who do not interact with clients are not charged under Standard V(B) with ensuring that others' disclosures to clients are sufficient.
rationales.B: Institutional clients are clients. A member whose firm serves only institutional accounts remains subject to Standard V(B); the absence of retail clients narrows neither the duty to distinguish fact from opinion nor the duty to disclose significant risks and limitations.
rationales.C: Generally, this standard affects only client-facing members. While CFA Institute encourages all investment professionals to help ensure that clients receive sufficient disclosures, the standard does not impose a duty on members and candidates who do not interact with clients to ensure that others comply with Standard V(B). As with other standards that may not be applicable to the professional responsibilities of all members and candidates, such as investment performance and suitability, those who are part of a team of investment professionals providing services to clients but who do not have client-facing responsibilities need not expand their realm of responsibility to ensure appropriate disclosures to clients.

questions.stem: A client's investment policy statement calls for a benchmark-oriented approach, and the benchmark carried a 35% technology weighting over the past three years. The client now complains about negative equity returns and about the portfolio's technology exposure. Under Standard V(C), the adviser was most likely required to have retained:

options.A: the policy statement and the benchmark's weighting records.
options.B: nothing beyond the executed trade tickets.
options.C: the documentation assembled if litigation follows.

rationales.A: Having appropriate records matters here because they show that over the past three years the portion of technology stocks in the benchmark index was 35%, as called for in the client's investment policy statement. To comply with Standard V(C), the adviser would have been required to retain the client's IPS stating that the benchmark was appropriate for the client's investment objectives. He would also have had to keep records indicating that the investment process was explained appropriately to the client and that the IPS was updated on a regular basis.
rationales.B: Trade tickets evidence what was executed but not why. The records that answer a complaint of this kind are the ones supporting the process: the IPS's benchmark-oriented requirement, the benchmark's own technology weighting, the explanation of the investment process given to the client, and the regular updating of the IPS.
rationales.C: The records must exist from the time of the analysis and the decisions; they cannot be assembled once a dispute arises. Standard V(C) requires documentation contemporaneous with the research and recommendations, so the duty attaches when the work is done and is unrelated to whether a client complaint turns into litigation.

questions.stem: An analyst writes numerous reports on luxury retail, drawing on interviews with company managers, manufacturers and economists, on-site visits, customer surveys, and secondary research by analysts covering related industries. Under Standard V(C), he is most likely required to retain:

options.A: none of the third-party research.
options.B: copies of every input, third-party research included.
options.C: only the documentation of his quantitative work.

rationales.A: An analyst who relies on third-party research must keep copies of it to support his own conclusions. Another analyst's retention practices are no substitute: the file that substantiates this analyst's report has to be his own, and failing to maintain it violates Standard V(C).
rationales.B: He must document and keep copies of all the information that goes into his reports, including the secondary or third-party research of other analysts. Failure to maintain such files would violate Standard V(C).
rationales.C: Every input to the reports must be documented and kept: the interviews, the on-site visits, the customer surveys and the secondary research alike. Qualitative work is documented through notes and memoranda of the interviews and visits, so the requirement is in no way confined to quantitative analysis.

questions.stem: An analyst documents the assumptions and reasoning behind an analytical model he develops while employed at a firm, then joins a competitor and takes copies of the supporting records with him. Under Standard V(C), those records are most likely:

options.A: his own, as he authored them.
options.B: his to take, as they name no client.
options.C: his former employer's property.

rationales.A: Records created in the course of employment are the employer's property regardless of who authored them. Authorship confers no ownership, and to go on using the model the analyst must recreate its supporting records at the new firm.
rationales.B: Firm ownership of the work product does not depend on the presence or absence of client identifiers. The model documentation belongs to the former employer whether or not any client is named in it.
rationales.C: The records created by the analyst supporting the research model he developed at his former firm are that firm's records. Taking the documents with him to his new employer without the former firm's permission violates Standard V(C). To use the model in the future, he must recreate the records supporting it at the new firm.

questions.stem: A member worked from home at weekends, saving correspondence and completed work on her home computer. After being released by the firm, she used those files to request recommendation letters from former clients and to show reports to prospective clients as examples of her abilities. Her conduct under Standard V(C) is most likely:

options.A: a violation, because she kept and used the files without her former employer's permission.
options.B: permissible, because the files were created on her own time and equipment.
options.C: a violation, because saving firm work on a home computer is prohibited.

rationales.A: She needed the permission of her employer to maintain the files at home after her employment ended; without that permission she should have deleted them. All files created as part of a member's or candidate's professional activity are the property of the firm, even those created outside normal work hours, so using them afterwards to solicit recommendations or to show prospective clients her work violates Standard V(C).
rationales.B: The files are firm property even though she created them on her own time and on her own computer. What makes them the firm's records is that they were produced as part of her professional activity; when and where the work was done is beside the point.
rationales.C: The Code and Standards do not prohibit using one's personal computer to complete work for one's employer. The violation lies in keeping and using the files after employment ended without permission, not in where the work was stored while she was employed.

questions.stem: A review of a holding leads a manager to make no change to the position. Under Standard V(C), the record-retention duty most likely:

options.A: extends to the review.
options.B: is triggered by execution.
options.C: reaches only reviews that lead to a trade.

rationales.A: Members and candidates must retain records that substantiate the scope of their research and the reasons for their actions or conclusions. The retention requirement applies to decisions to buy or sell a security as well as to reviews undertaken that do not lead to a change in position.
rationales.B: The decision to hold is itself an investment conclusion, and the records must support it. Execution is not what triggers the duty; the scope of the research and the reasoning behind the conclusion are what have to be documented.
rationales.C: Records must substantiate the scope of research and the reasons for actions or conclusions, conclusions not to act included. Tying the duty to a trade would leave every hold decision undocumented, which is precisely the gap the standard closes by naming reviews that do not lead to a change in position.

questions.stem: A member joins a new firm and wishes to use research reports and recommendations she prepared at a previous employer, whose supporting documentation stayed behind. Under Standard V(C), that use is most likely:

options.A: prohibited until the records are recreated.
options.B: permitted on her attestation that records once existed.
options.C: permitted on the ground that the analysis was her own.

rationales.A: Members and candidates must not use historical recommendations or research reports created at a previous firm if the supporting documentation is unavailable. For future use of any work from a previous firm on behalf of a new employer, members and candidates must recreate the supporting records at the new firm; however, these new records cannot be recreated from sources obtained at a previous employer without that employer's permission.
rationales.B: An attestation from memory does not replace supporting records. The reasonable basis has to be re-created at the new firm from new or properly obtained documentation before the prior work may be relied on again.
rationales.C: Without the supporting documentation the prior recommendations and reports may not be used. Authorship is beside the point: the records are the former employer's property and stayed with it, so the basis must be rebuilt at the new firm rather than assumed.

questions.stem: In the absence of regulatory guidance or firm policy, the record-retention period recommended under Standard V(C) is most likely:

options.A: no recommended minimum.
options.B: at least one year.
options.C: at least seven years.

rationales.A: A default does exist. Where neither regulation nor firm policy specifies a period, CFA Institute recommends retaining records for at least seven years, so the question is not left wholly to the member's judgment.
rationales.B: The recommended default is materially longer than a year: at least seven years where there is no regulatory guidance and no firm policy on retention.
rationales.C: In the absence of regulatory guidance or firm policies, CFA Institute recommends maintaining records for at least seven years. Where local regulation or a firm's own policy does specify a period, that requirement governs; the seven-year recommendation fills the gap when neither does.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(B), the risks a member is required to disclose at the time of a recommendation are most likely:

options.A: the significant risks known to the member.
options.B: all risks, however immaterial or remote.
options.C: the risks not already known to the public.

rationales.A: Members and candidates must disclose significant risks known to them at the time of the disclosure. They cannot be expected to disclose risks they are unaware of at the time recommendations or investment actions are made. In assessing compliance with Standard V(B), it is important to establish knowledge of a purported significant risk or limitation: having no knowledge of a risk or limitation that subsequently triggers a loss may reveal a deficiency in the diligence and reasonable basis of the member's or candidate's research, but it may not constitute a breach of Standard V(B).
rationales.B: The duty extends only to significant risks known to the member at the time of the disclosure. Remote and immaterial risks, and risks the member could not have known of, fall outside it, which is why establishing knowledge matters in assessing compliance.
rationales.C: Public knowledge of a risk does not discharge the duty. Significant risks material to the recommendation must still be disclosed to the client, whatever their circulation elsewhere; the limit on the duty is the member's knowledge, not the client's opportunity to learn of the risk independently.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(B), a member's duty to disclose the nature of services provided and the costs charged is most likely:

options.A: ongoing throughout the client relationship.
options.B: triggered by a specific client request.
options.C: complete once made at account opening.

rationales.A: The disclosure responsibilities of members and candidates under Standard V(B) are ongoing. Initial disclosures made at the outset of the relationship alone may not meet the requirements of the standard, because the information a client needs in order to judge the value of the services and the cost of obtaining them changes as the arrangement changes. If the services or the costs change, members and candidates must update the disclosures and provide the updated information to all affected clients and prospective clients on a timely basis.
rationales.B: Disclosure under Standard V(B) is affirmative and proactive, not request-driven. A client who does not know what services are being performed or what is being charged for them has no reason to ask for an itemization, so treating a client request as the trigger would defeat the purpose of the standard. The member must disclose without being asked, and must keep the disclosure current as services and costs change.
rationales.C: Disclosure at account opening does not complete the duty. The responsibility is ongoing: initial disclosures at the outset of the relationship may not meet the requirements of the standard, and any change in the services provided or the costs charged obliges the member to update the disclosures and deliver the updated information to all affected clients and prospective clients on a timely basis.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(B), the scope of a member's cost disclosures to a client is most likely:

options.A: all costs of the services, including affiliate and third-party charges.
options.B: the contracting entity's fees, with affiliate charges disclosed on request.
options.C: the fees charged by the contracting entity.

rationales.A: The scope of the disclosures is not limited to only those costs charged by the entity with which the client is in a direct relationship. Members and candidates with client-facing responsibilities must provide disclosures about all the costs associated with the investment services and products provided to the client. Those disclosures include information on costs arising from services provided by affiliates, related entities, or third parties for products and services used by members, candidates, or their firms in providing services to clients.
rationales.B: Cost disclosure under Standard V(B) is affirmative rather than request-driven. Clients who are not told that affiliates, related entities, or third parties are being paid out of the arrangement have no basis on which to request an itemization of those charges, so holding affiliate charges back until the client asks withholds exactly the information the standard requires. All costs associated with the services and products provided must be disclosed whether or not the client asks.
rationales.C: The scope of disclosure is not limited to the entity with which the client is in a direct relationship. Members and candidates with client-facing responsibilities must disclose all the costs associated with the investment services and products provided, including costs arising from services provided by affiliates, related entities, or third parties for products and services used by the member, candidate, or firm in serving the client. Confining disclosure to the contracting entity's own fees understates what the client pays.

drills.los_text: recommend practices and procedures designed to prevent violations of the Code and Standards
drills.reading_name: Guidance for Standard V: Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions

questions.stem: Under Standard V(A), a member's opinion on whether third-party research is sound is most likely based on:

options.A: the provider's process as it stood when the subscription began.
options.B: the reputation of the firm publishing the research.
options.C: the assumptions, rigor, timeliness, and objectivity of the work.

rationales.A: Soundness has to be assessed on an ongoing basis rather than once at the outset. The criteria themselves make this clear: one of them is the date and timeliness of the research, and a provider's assumptions, the rigor of its analysis, and the objectivity and independence of its recommendations can all deteriorate over time. An opinion resting on the provider's process as it stood when the subscription began says nothing about the research being relied on today.
rationales.B: Reputation is not the test. The criteria that a member or candidate may use in forming an opinion on whether research is sound are the assumptions used, the rigor of the analysis performed, the date and timeliness of the research, and an evaluation of the objectivity and independence of the recommendations. A well-regarded firm can still publish research built on stale data or conflicted recommendations, so the member must examine the work itself.
rationales.C: Criteria that a member or candidate may use in forming an opinion on whether research is sound include, but are not limited to: the assumptions used; the rigor of the analysis performed; the date and timeliness of the research; and an evaluation of the objectivity and independence of the recommendations. These go to the substance of the work and to whether it can still be relied on, which is what a reasonable and adequate basis requires.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(A), the testing of a preprogrammed analytical tool's output is most likely:

options.A: performed by the member before the tool is relied on.
options.B: performed by the technology staff who coded the tool.
options.C: performed by the member once live results accumulate.

rationales.A: Members and candidates must make reasonable efforts to test the output of investment models and other preprogrammed analytical tools they use, and such validation must occur before incorporating the process into their methods, models, or analyses. Testing in advance is what allows the member to claim a reasonable and adequate basis for the recommendations the tool helps produce.
rationales.B: The duty attaches to the member who uses the model, not to whoever built or coded it. Members and candidates must make reasonable efforts to test the output of the investment models and preprogrammed analytical tools they use; leaving the work to the developers does not relieve the user of that responsibility, because it is the user who relies on the output in forming recommendations.
rationales.C: Validation must occur before the process is incorporated into the member's methods, models, or analyses, not after it is already in service. Waiting for live results means client recommendations are being made on untested output in the interim, which is precisely the exposure the reasonable-basis requirement is meant to prevent. Live performance is not a substitute for testing beforehand.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(A), the assumptions a member's investment analysis incorporates are most likely:

options.A: the base case the member judges most probable.
options.B: a range of scenarios drawn from normal market conditions.
options.C: a broad range that includes negative market events.

rationales.A: A base case on its own, however probable, is not sufficient. Members and candidates must ensure that their analyses incorporate a broad range of assumptions sufficient to capture the underlying characteristics of the investment. An analysis that fails to consider potentially negative outcomes, or levels of risk outside the norm, may not accurately measure the true economic value of the investment.
rationales.B: Confining the range to normal conditions is the defect, not the remedy. Analysis that fails to consider potentially negative outcomes or levels of risk outside the norm may not accurately measure the true economic value of an investment. In reviewing computer models and their output, members and candidates must include the factors and assumptions likely to have a substantial influence on value, ensuring a wide range of possible input expectations that reaches beyond the normal case to negative market events.
rationales.C: Although not every model tests for every factor or outcome, members and candidates must ensure that their analyses incorporate a broad range of assumptions sufficient to capture the underlying characteristics of investments.
