Analysis that fails to consider potentially negative outcomes or levels of risk outside the norm may not accurately measure the true economic value of an investment. In reviewing computer models or the resulting output, members and candidates must include factors and assumptions likely to have a substantial influence on an investment's value, so that the model incorporates a wide range of possible input expectations, including negative market events.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(A), the criteria a member applies in selecting an external adviser or subadviser most likely include:

options.A: a review of the adviser's established code of ethics.
options.B: a ranking of the candidates by management fee.
options.C: nothing beyond a comparison of net-of-fee return records.

rationales.A: The criteria a member or candidate applies in selecting an external adviser or subadviser include, but are not limited to: reviewing the adviser's established code of ethics; understanding the adviser's compliance and internal control procedures; assessing the quality of the published return information; and reviewing the adviser's investment process and its adherence to the stated strategy. The code of ethics review is one of those elements.
rationales.B: Fee level is a commercial term of the mandate, not one of the criteria the guidance names. The selection must rest on a review of the adviser's established code of ethics, an understanding of its compliance and internal control procedures, an assessment of the quality of its published return information, and a review of its investment process and adherence to the stated strategy. Ranking candidates by fee leaves all of that unexamined.
rationales.C: The quality of published return information is only one of the criteria. The review must also cover the adviser's established code of ethics, its compliance and internal control procedures, and its investment process and adherence to the stated strategy. A return comparison on its own says nothing about how those returns were generated or whether the process that produced them will persist.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(A), a firm's recommended policies on the basis for recommendations are most likely:

options.A: waived for analysts with established professional experience.
options.B: confined to equity research.
options.C: applied to research reports, credit ratings, and recommendations.

rationales.A: Experience does not earn a waiver from a documented policy. The recommended practice is to establish policies requiring that research reports, credit ratings, and investment recommendations have a basis that can be substantiated as reasonable and adequate, and to develop detailed, written guidance setting out the due diligence procedures for judging whether a particular recommendation meets that test. Written policies make the standard auditable regardless of who performs the work.
rationales.B: The coverage is not confined to equity research. The recommended policies reach research reports, credit ratings, and investment recommendations alike, each of which must have a basis that can be substantiated as reasonable and adequate. A credit rating issued without such a basis is as much a breach as an equity recommendation issued without one.
rationales.C: Recommended practices under Standard V(A) include establishing policies requiring that research reports, credit ratings, and investment recommendations have a basis that can be substantiated as reasonable and adequate; developing detailed, written guidance that establishes the due diligence procedures for judging whether a particular recommendation has a reasonable and adequate basis; and developing measurable criteria for assessing the quality of research, the reasonableness and adequacy of the basis for any recommendation or rating, and the accuracy of recommendations over time.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(A), a firm's recommended guidance on scenario testing of computer-based models is most likely:

options.A: written for vendor-supplied models and silent on in-house ones.
options.B: detailed and written, setting minimum testing levels.
options.C: general, leaving the extent of testing to each analyst.

rationales.A: Internally developed models are covered on the same footing as purchased ones, and arguably attract more scrutiny, since the firm that builds a model is responsible for its assumptions as well as its output. Guidance that speaks only to vendor-supplied models leaves the firm's own models untested. The recommended guidance applies to all computer-based models used in developing, rating, and evaluating financial instruments, whatever their source.
rationales.B: The recommended practice is to develop detailed, written guidance that establishes minimum levels of scenario testing of all computer-based models used in developing, rating, and evaluating financial instruments. The policy should contain criteria related to the breadth of the scenarios tested, the accuracy of the output over time, and the analysis of cash flow sensitivity to inputs.
rationales.C: Leaving the extent of testing to each analyst is the opposite of what is recommended. The guidance is to be detailed and written, and to establish minimum levels of scenario testing for all computer-based models used in developing, rating, and evaluating financial instruments, with criteria covering the breadth of scenarios tested, the accuracy of output over time, and cash flow sensitivity to inputs. Guidance pitched at a general level sets no minimum at all and cannot be reviewed for compliance.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(A), the criteria a firm uses to assess its outside information providers are most likely based on:

options.A: the price of the service relative to competing vendors.
options.B: information quality, collection practices, and accuracy.
options.C: the length and strength of the business relationship.

rationales.A: Price is not one of the dimensions the recommended practice names. The criteria are to be measurable and to address the quality of the information provided, the reasonableness and adequacy of the provider's information collection practices, and the accuracy of the information over time. A cheaper feed that is carelessly collected or inaccurate fails every one of those tests, so price tells the firm nothing about whether the information can support a reasonable and adequate basis.
rationales.B: The recommended practice is to develop measurable criteria for assessing outside providers, including the quality of the information being provided, the reasonableness and adequacy of the provider's information collection practices, and the accuracy of the information over time. The established policy should also outline how often the provider's products are reviewed.
rationales.C: Longevity of the relationship is not a measure of information quality; it is a reason the quality may never have been questioned. The practice calls for measurable criteria covering the quality of the information provided, the reasonableness and adequacy of the provider's collection practices, and the accuracy of that information over time, together with a stated frequency for reviewing the provider's products.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(A), the recommended basis for evaluating the adequacy of external advisers and subadvisers is most likely:

options.A: case-specific judgment applied to each adviser.
options.B: a consistent, objective set of criteria.
options.C: criteria applied once at appointment and not revisited.

rationales.A: Discretionary judgment formed case by case is not the recommended approach, because it cannot be applied evenly across advisers or defended after the fact. The practice is to adopt a consistent, objective set of criteria for evaluating the adequacy of external advisers and subadvisers, and to set out how often and on what basis allocations to them will be reviewed.
rationales.B: The recommended practice is to adopt a consistent, objective set of criteria for evaluating the adequacy of external advisers and subadvisers. The policy should also include how often, and on what basis, the allocation of funds to the external adviser or subadviser will be reviewed.
rationales.C: One review at appointment is not sufficient. Beyond adopting consistent, objective criteria, the policy should specify how often and on what basis the allocation of funds to the external adviser or subadviser will be reviewed, which makes the evaluation a continuing obligation rather than a one-time gate at appointment.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(A), an external adviser's voluntary adherence to recognized industry standards such as the CFA Institute Asset Manager Code or GIPS is most likely:

options.A: one factor in the adviser's evaluation.
options.B: no factor in the adviser's evaluation.
options.C: the only factor in the adviser's evaluation.

rationales.A: One factor in evaluating external advisers or subadvisers is whether they adhere to recognized industry standards to guide their work. Codes, standards, and guides on best practice published by CFA Institute establish practices for advisers and may be used by members and candidates as criteria for selecting external advisers or subadvisers. Those available at the CFA Institute Research and Policy Center website include the CFA Institute Asset Manager Code, the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS), and the Model Request for Proposal for equity, credit, or real estate managers. Adherence is therefore one input into the diligence Standard V(A) requires, used alongside review of the adviser's compliance culture, code of ethics, and the quality of the information and analysis it produces.
rationales.B: Voluntariness does not diminish the signal. A firm's commitment to recognized industry standards is observable evidence about how it conducts its work, and the Standard V(A) guidance on selecting external advisers and subadvisers names such standards as criteria members and candidates may use in making the selection. Treating adherence as irrelevant discards information the diligence assessment is supposed to weigh.
rationales.C: Adherence to recognized industry standards is one factor in evaluating an external adviser, not a substitute for the broader review. A member relying on an adviser or subadviser still has to assess the adviser's compliance culture, its code of ethics, and the reasonableness and quality of the information it supplies. A claim of Asset Manager Code or GIPS compliance narrows the inquiry but does not discharge it, so further diligence remains necessary.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(A), the level of review a member or candidate must undertake on information and data used in analysis is most likely:

options.A: lower for public online sources than for proprietary data.
options.B: influenced by the source of the information.
options.C: uniform across all sources.

rationales.A: Public availability does not lower the bar. The guidance runs the other way: information and data taken from sources such as blogs, independent research aggregation websites, or social media may require a greater level of review than information from more established research organizations, precisely because wide circulation is not evidence that anyone has verified the material. Being freely accessible says nothing about diligence already performed on it.
rationales.B: The sources of the information and data will influence the level of the review a member or candidate must undertake. Information and data taken from certain sources, such as blogs, independent research aggregation websites, or social media, may require a greater level of review than information from more established research organizations. The diligence obligation is calibrated to how much comfort the source itself supplies: a less-established source leaves more of the verification work to the member or candidate.
rationales.C: Review is not uniform. Standard V(A) guidance on information sources makes the required level of review depend on where the information came from, with less-established sources such as blogs, aggregation websites, and social media warranting greater scrutiny than more established research organizations. A single fixed level of review would either waste effort on well-vetted material or leave weakly sourced material unchecked.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(B), the best-practice vehicle and timing for describing the nature, parameters, and costs of professional services to a client is most likely:

options.A: in writing at the outset of the engagement.
options.B: in writing after the engagement concludes.
options.C: verbally at the first client meeting.

rationales.A: Best practice is for members and candidates with client-facing responsibilities to clearly set out in written form at the outset of the engagement a description of the nature and parameters of the professional services, as part of the engagement agreement, contract, or other documents stipulating the terms of the client relationship. Doing so at the start gives the client the information while the decision to engage is still open, and recording it in writing documents for both parties what the client was told.
rationales.B: Disclosure at the outset is the point of the requirement: the client needs the description of services and costs before deciding to engage, not after. Where exact totals cannot be known in advance, such as a fee based on the quarterly market value of assets under management, the answer is to supply a reasonable amount of detail and expected ranges at the start rather than to defer disclosure until the engagement has ended.
rationales.C: A verbal explanation at the first meeting may usefully supplement the disclosure, but best practice under Standard V(B) is written form at the outset, incorporated into the engagement agreement, contract, or other documents stipulating the terms of the client relationship. Writing, not conversation, is what creates a durable record of the nature and parameters of the services the client agreed to.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(B), the cost information a member or candidate must provide to a client is most likely:

options.A: the firm's internal cost of providing the services.
options.B: reasonable detail without specific dollar amounts.
options.C: a specific dollar figure for all costs in advance.

rationales.A: Members and candidates are not required to disclose a description of the costs to the firm of providing those services. What the standard reaches is the costs the client will incur, described in a reasonable amount of detail. The firm's own cost of production is outside the disclosure obligation.
rationales.B: Members and candidates should provide a reasonable amount of detail regarding the costs to be incurred by clients. The standard, however, does not require members and candidates to provide specific dollar amounts. For example, a firm that charges clients a quarterly fee based on the market value of assets under management will be unable to specify a dollar amount in advance, since the fee depends on a value not yet known. Members and candidates are also not required to disclose a description of the costs to the firm of providing those services.
rationales.C: A specific dollar figure often cannot be given in advance. A firm charging a quarterly fee based on the market value of assets under management cannot know the amount until the valuation date, so requiring a dollar figure before the engagement begins would be impossible to satisfy. The standard calls for a reasonable amount of detail about the costs the client will incur, not an exact amount.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(B), disclosure to clients of a firm's use of external advisers is most likely required:

options.A: only when they manage a majority of client assets.
options.B: only at account opening.
options.C: whenever external advisers form part of the investment process.

rationales.A: There is no majority or materiality threshold. External advisers managing various portions of clients' assets under management must be disclosed as part of the investment process regardless of the share of assets they manage, because the disclosure exists to let clients understand the full mix of products and strategies being applied to their objectives.
rationales.B: The duty to keep clients informed about the investment process is ongoing rather than a one-time formality at account opening. Engaging a new external adviser changes the investment process, and clients need that information to understand the strategies being applied and the manager's reliance on other investment professionals.
rationales.C: A firm's investment process may include the use of external advisers to manage various portions of clients' assets under management, and members and candidates must inform clients about the use of external advisers as part of their investment process. This disclosure allows clients to understand the full mix of products and strategies being applied that may affect their investment objectives. It also provides insight into the capabilities of the investment manager and the manager's reliance on other investment professionals to provide services.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(B), disclosure of the risks associated with leverage and other complex financial instruments is most likely:

options.A: limited to reporting realized losses.
options.B: required where those risks are significant.
options.C: optional for sophisticated clients.

rationales.A: The duty is prospective risk disclosure, not after-the-fact loss reporting. Clients need to understand the general market-related risks and the risks of complex instruments before committing capital, which is when the information can still affect the investment decision. Reporting losses once they have been realized comes too late to serve that purpose.
rationales.B: Members and candidates must adequately disclose the general market-related risks and the risks associated with the use of complex financial instruments that are deemed significant. Other types of risks that members and candidates may consider disclosing include but are not limited to counterparty risk, country risk, sector or industry risk, security-specific risk, and credit risk. In general, the use of leverage constitutes a significant risk and must be disclosed.
rationales.C: Client sophistication does not remove the obligation. The use of leverage in general constitutes a significant risk and must be disclosed, as must the other general market-related risks and complex-instrument risks deemed significant. Presuming that a sophisticated client already understands the risk substitutes the manager's assumption for the disclosure the standard requires.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(B), the liquidity and capacity characteristics of an investment security or vehicle are most likely:

options.A: limiting factors that must be reported when significant.
options.B: competitive information that may be withheld from clients.
options.C: universal risks that need no specific disclosure.

rationales.A: Investment securities and vehicles may have limiting factors that influence a client's or prospective client's investment decision, and members and candidates must report to clients and prospective clients the existence of limitations significant to the decision-making process. Examples of such factors and attributes include but are not limited to investment liquidity and capacity. Liquidity is the ability to liquidate an investment on a timely basis at a reasonable cost; capacity is the investment amount beyond which returns will be negatively affected by new investments.
rationales.B: Capacity is the investment amount beyond which returns will be negatively affected by new investments, so a capacity constraint bears directly on the returns a client can expect. A limitation significant to the client's decision-making process must be reported; its commercial sensitivity does not make it withholdable.
rationales.C: That every investment carries some liquidity risk is not a reason to stay silent about a particular one. Liquidity, the ability to liquidate an investment on a timely basis at a reasonable cost, is given as an example of a limiting factor that can influence the investment decision, and limitations significant to the decision-making process must be reported to clients and prospective clients.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(B), reference material supporting investment advice based on quantitative research and analysis is most likely:

options.A: unnecessary for proprietary models.
options.B: required only for regulatory examinations.
options.C: required to be readily available.

rationales.A: A proprietary model does not exempt the advice it produces from support. Members and candidates must support investment advice based on quantitative research and analysis with readily available reference material, and must also disclose any changes in methodology. Confidentiality of the model's internals does not relieve the obligation to have supporting material on hand.
rationales.B: The support must be readily available as a matter of course, not assembled when a regulator asks. The obligation attaches to the giving of the advice, so the reference material has to exist and be accessible at that point; material produced only in response to an examination is not readily available.
rationales.C: Members and candidates must support investment advice based on quantitative research and analysis with readily available reference material. Members and candidates must also disclose any changes in methodology. Keeping the supporting material readily available lets clients and others understand the basis of the advice, and the methodology-change disclosure keeps them informed when the basis itself shifts.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(B), a recommendation communicated in abbreviated form, such as a recommended stock list, is most likely:

options.A: complete in itself, imposing no further duty.
options.B: acceptable with notice that further analysis is available.
options.C: prohibited for lack of an adequate basis.

rationales.A: An abbreviated format does not stand alone. If recommendations are contained in abbreviated form, such as a recommended stock list, members and candidates should notify clients that additional information and analyses are available from the producer of the report, so that a client who wants the basis for a recommendation knows it can be obtained.
rationales.B: If recommendations are contained in abbreviated form, such as a recommended stock list, members and candidates should notify clients that additional information and analyses are available from the producer of the report. The short format is permitted; what it carries with it is the notice that the supporting information and analyses exist and can be requested from the producer.
rationales.C: Abbreviated formats are not prohibited. A recommended stock list may be distributed provided clients are notified that additional information and analyses are available from the producer of the report; the supporting work exists and is obtainable, so the brief format does not leave the recommendation without a basis.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(B), provided the required disclosures are appropriate, accurate, timely, and complete, the manner of their delivery is most likely:

options.A: restricted to verbal delivery.
options.B: fixed by a single prescribed template.
options.C: at the member's discretion.

rationales.A: The manner of disclosure is at the member's or candidate's individual discretion, so verbal delivery is not mandated. Best practice in fact points the other way, dictating that such disclosures be made in written form, which creates a record of what the client was told; the governing test is that the disclosures be appropriate, accurate, timely, and complete.
rationales.B: No template is prescribed. The manner in which members and candidates provide the disclosures required by Standard V(B) is at their individual discretion, and what must be satisfied is the quality of the disclosure rather than its format: appropriate, accurate, timely, and complete, with written form as best practice.
rationales.C: The manner in which members and candidates provide the disclosures required by Standard V(B) is at their individual discretion so long as the disclosures are appropriate, accurate, timely, and complete. Best practice dictates that such disclosures be made in written form. Discretion over format is therefore bounded by those four qualities, not by a mandated vehicle.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(B), a member who is directed to use firm-generated disclosures that are inadequate most likely must:

options.A: keep silent, since firmwide consistency comes first.
options.B: defer to the firm, which bears the responsibility.
options.C: ensure the disclosures meet the Code and Standards.

rationales.A: Consistency across the firm is not a reason for silence, and silence is not the member's recourse. Standard V(B) sets out an escalation path instead: alert the firm when the communication is lacking, flawed, or insufficient; supplement the disclosure where that is possible; and, if inadequate disclosures mandated by the firm cannot be rectified or supplemented, document the objection and take steps to dissociate from the activity.
rationales.B: Members and candidates may rely on firm-generated disclosures and can be directed to use them, but that direction does not shift responsibility onto the firm. The member must still ensure that the disclosures used with clients meet the requirements of the Code and Standards, and must alert the firm when they do not.
rationales.C: Standard V(B) guidance on the manner of disclosure states: 'While members and candidates rely on and can be directed to use firm-generated disclosures, members and candidates should ensure that these disclosures meet the requirements of the Code and Standards. They have the responsibility to alert their firm when the communication is lacking, flawed, or insufficient to meet their responsibilities under the Code and Standards. In such cases, members and candidates should, when possible, supplement disclosures from the firm that they consider insufficient to meet the requirements of this standard. Ultimately, if members and candidates cannot rectify or supplement inadequate disclosures mandated by the firm, they should document their objections and take steps to dissociate from the activity.' The duty to ensure adequacy therefore stays with the member, backed by an escalation path of alert, supplement, document, and dissociate.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(B), whether a member exercised reasonable judgment in including and excluding information in a research report is most likely assessed through:

options.A: a per se rule against omitting factors.
options.B: a standardized industry checklist.
options.C: case-by-case review of the report's facts.

rationales.A: Leaving a factor out of a report is not itself a violation. Research reports necessarily omit less-important factors, and the standard asks only whether the member's judgment about what to include and exclude was reasonable.
rationales.B: No specific checklist governs the choice of factors. Because selecting relevant factors is an analytical skill, the determination depends on case-by-case review rather than on a standard list of items, though members should encourage their firms to adopt a rigorous methodology for reviewing research created for publication and dissemination to clients.
rationales.C: Standard V(B) compliance practices state: 'Because the selection of relevant factors is an analytical skill, determination of whether a member or candidate has used reasonable judgment in excluding and including information in research reports depends heavily on case-by-case reviews rather than a specific checklist. Members and candidates should encourage their firms to have a rigorous methodology for reviewing research that is created for publication and dissemination to clients.' The analytical nature of factor selection is what makes a single checklist inadequate as the test of reasonable judgment.

questions.stem: A member's obligation under Standard V(B) with respect to the records supporting a released research report is most likely to:

options.A: maintain them and supply information on request.
options.B: furnish them to examining regulators but not clients.
options.C: discard them once the report is distributed.

rationales.A: Standard V(B) compliance practices state: 'To assist in the review of a report after its release, the member or candidate must maintain records indicating the nature of the research and should, if asked, be able to supply additional information to the client (or any user of the report) covering factors not included in the report.' The records must therefore survive publication, and the member must remain able to explain factors the report itself left out.
rationales.B: Regulators are not the only audience for the supporting information. The member should be able to supply additional information to the client, or to any other user of the report, on request, covering factors not included in the report itself.
rationales.C: Records indicating the nature of the research must be maintained after release, precisely so that the report can be reviewed later and factors not included in it can be explained. Discarding the supporting records defeats that purpose and leaves the member unable to answer a client's request for additional information.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(B), a member who distributes investment information to clients in electronic or digital format most likely:

options.A: is free to favor premium-tier clients.
options.B: need not weigh fair dealing when delivery is instant.
options.C: must take reasonable steps to treat all clients fairly.

rationales.A: Giving one tier of clients earlier or better access to a recommendation is exactly the unfairness the guidance targets. The delivery channel may not be used as a service differentiator for investment recommendations.
rationales.B: Speed of distribution does not guarantee equal access, so digital delivery is not exempt. Electronic and digital delivery still requires reasonable steps to ensure that all intended recipients are treated fairly, and social media services in particular may not be available to every client.
rationales.C: Standard V(B) guidance states: 'When providing information to clients in electronic or digital format, members and candidates must take reasonable steps to ensure that such delivery treats all clients fairly. Members and candidates using any social media service to communicate business information must be diligent in their efforts to avoid unintended problems because these services may not be available to all clients.' Fair treatment of all clients is the test the delivery method has to satisfy.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(C), supporting documentation retained for an investment recommendation most likely includes:

options.A: trade tickets and transaction confirmations and nothing else.
options.B: internally generated records, excluding outside research.
options.C: personal notes from meetings with the covered company.

rationales.A: Supporting documentation runs much wider than transaction paperwork. The examples include personal notes from meetings with the covered company, press releases or presentations issued by that company, computer-based model outputs and analyses, computer-based model input parameters, risk analyses of securities' impacts on a portfolio, selection criteria for external advisers, notes from meetings with clients, and outside research reports.
rationales.B: Outside research reports are expressly listed among the examples of supporting documentation, so the record is not confined to material the firm generated itself. Third-party work relied on in the analysis has to be retained alongside internal notes and model output.
rationales.C: Standard V(C) guidance states: 'The following are examples of supporting documentation that assists the member or candidate in meeting the requirements for record retention: personal notes from meetings with the covered company, press releases or presentations issued by the covered company, computer-based model outputs and analyses, computer-based model input parameters, risk analyses of securities' impacts on a portfolio, selection criteria for external advisers, notes from meetings with clients, and outside research reports.' Personal meeting notes sit at the head of that list.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(C), the electronic or digital records a member must retain most likely include:

options.A: electronic records other than informal messaging and posts.
options.B: emails, text messages, blog posts, and social media posts.
options.C: formal email correspondence, and no other format.

rationales.A: Informal electronic channels are not carved out of the retention requirement. Text messages, blog posts, and social media posts are expressly named among the electronic and digital formats that must be retained when they hold information used in analysis or communicated to clients.
rationales.B: Standard V(C) guidance states: 'Examples of electronic or digital formats for records that must be retained include but are not limited to emails, text messages, blog posts, and social media posts.' The list is illustrative rather than exhaustive, so newer channels used to carry business communication fall under the same duty, and the informality of the medium is no exemption.
rationales.C: Email is only one of the named formats. Text messages, blog posts, and social media posts must be retained as well, so limiting retention to formal email correspondence leaves out records the standard requires.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(C), gathering and sharing information through electronic and online formats most likely:

options.A: creates challenges in keeping appropriate records.
options.B: makes messaging content too transient to retain.
options.C: leaves that information outside record keeping.

rationales.A: Standard V(C) guidance states: 'Electronic and online formats for gathering and sharing information create challenges in maintaining the appropriate records and files. The nature or format of the information does not remove members' and candidates' responsibility to maintain a record of information used in their analysis or communicated to clients.' The format changes the difficulty of compliance, not the underlying duty.
rationales.B: Transience of the medium is not an exemption, and messaging content is no less capturable than any other. Content used in professional analysis, or communicated to clients, must still be captured in appropriate records whatever channel carried it, because the nature or format of the information does not remove the responsibility to keep a record.
rationales.C: Electronic and online formats make record maintenance harder; they do not excuse it. The nature or format of the information does not remove members' and candidates' responsibility to maintain a record of what was used in their analysis or communicated to clients.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(C), records a member creates as part of professional activity on behalf of an employer are most likely the property of:

options.A: the author.
options.B: the departing member.
options.C: the employing firm.

rationales.A: Authorship does not confer ownership. Records created as part of a member's professional activity on behalf of the employer are, as a general matter, the property of the firm rather than of the analyst who prepared them.
rationales.B: Leaving does not transfer ownership. Members and candidates who leave a firm to seek other employment cannot take firm property, including original forms or copies of supporting records of their work, to the new employer without the express consent of the previous employer.
rationales.C: Standard V(C) guidance on records as property of the firm states: 'As a general matter, records created as part of members' and candidates' professional activity on behalf of their employer are the property of the firm. When members and candidates leave a firm to seek other employment, they cannot take the property of the firm, including original forms or copies of supporting records of their work, to the new employer without the express consent of the previous employer.'

questions.stem: Under Standard V(C), responsibility for maintaining the records that support investment action most likely rests with:

options.A: the firm rather than individuals.
options.B: individuals rather than their firm.
options.C: individuals, who must duplicate firm records.

rationales.A: Standard V(C) compliance practices state: 'The responsibility to maintain records that support investment action generally rests with the firm rather than individuals. Members and candidates should, however, archive research notes and other documents, either electronically or in hard copy, that support their current investment-related communications even if it is not required by the firm. Doing so will assist their firms in complying with requirements for preservation of internal or external records.' The firm carries the obligation, and personal archiving is recommended practice layered on top of it.
rationales.B: The general rule runs the other way: maintenance responsibility rests with the firm. Individual archiving of research notes and supporting documents is encouraged as a supplement, even where the firm does not require it, but it is not the whole of the duty.
rationales.C: Members and candidates are encouraged to archive the notes and documents supporting their own current investment-related communications, electronically or in hard copy. Duplicating the firm's records is not what the standard asks, because the maintenance responsibility generally rests with the firm rather than with individuals.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(C), the duty to be aware of and understand employer policies and regulatory rules on record retention most likely applies to:

options.A: all members and candidates.
options.B: the firm's records department.
options.C: members with supervisory responsibility.

rationales.A: Standard V(C) guidance on firm and regulatory requirements states: 'Members and candidates must be aware of and understand employer policies and regulatory rules relating to record retention. However, these policies and regulations may lag behind the advent of new communication methods, which places a greater responsibility on the individual for retaining all relevant records.' Because the written rules trail new communication channels, the individual's own awareness is what fills the gap.
rationales.B: The duty is personal and cannot be delegated to a records function. Each member and candidate must be aware of and understand the employer policies and regulatory rules that govern retention of the records their own work produces or relies on.
rationales.C: Supervisory status is not the trigger. The awareness requirement reaches every member and candidate whose work generates or relies on records, and the lag between retention policies and new communication methods places still greater responsibility on the individual.

questions.stem: A member retains research and client communication records for the time frames set by her local regulator and by her firm's own policy. Under Standard V(C), she has most likely:

options.A: satisfied those rules but not the standard itself.
options.B: satisfied the standard's retention requirement in full.
options.C: satisfied a benchmark that the standard leaves optional.

rationales.A: Standard V(C) imposes no residual retention obligation beyond what regulators and the firm require. Local regulators often impose requirements on members, candidates, and their firms related to record retention time frames that members and candidates must follow, and firms may also implement policies detailing the applicable time frame for retaining research and client communication records. Fulfilling such regulatory and firm requirements satisfies the requirements of Standard V(C), so there is no additional, undefined obligation left over for the member to meet.
rationales.B: Local regulators often impose requirements on members, candidates, and their firms related to record retention time frames that members and candidates must follow. Firms may also implement policies detailing the applicable time frame for retaining research and client communication records. Fulfilling such regulatory and firm requirements satisfies the requirements of Standard V(C): compliance with the applicable regulatory and firm retention rules is itself compliance with the standard, and the member need not identify some further period of her own.
rationales.C: Local regulatory retention requirements are binding where they apply, not optional benchmarks a member may set aside and replace with his or her own judgment. Members and candidates must follow the retention time frames regulators impose, and firms may add their own policies on top of them; it is precisely the fulfillment of those requirements that satisfies Standard V(C).

questions.stem: The scope of a member's record retention obligation under Standard V(C) is best described as:

options.A: dependent on whether a member manages portfolios.
options.B: dependent on one record list that binds every member.
options.C: dependent on the member's role in the decision process.

rationales.A: The obligation is not confined to portfolio managers. Which records are required to support recommendations or investment actions depends on the role of the member or candidate in the investment decision-making process, so research analysts, portfolio managers, and others each retain the records appropriate to their own role: the analyst keeps the research and support for the recommendation, the manager keeps the support for the investment action taken.
rationales.B: There is no one universal set of records that applies to every member regardless of function. The required records depend on the member's or candidate's role in the investment decision-making process; a research analyst's supporting records will differ from a portfolio manager's, because the obligation attaches to the artifacts that substantiate that individual's own scope of work and reasoning.
rationales.C: Which records are required to support recommendations or investment actions depends on the role of the member or candidate in the investment decision-making process. A research analyst's supporting records will differ from a portfolio manager's: the retention obligation applies to the artifacts that substantiate that individual's scope of work and reasoning, rather than to a fixed list applied uniformly across every function in the firm.
